blogs.title: "I'm Sensing That We Almost Need": The Seventh Circuit on Coercive Language and Fourth Amendment Consent
blogs.description: This post analyzes the court's handling of the voluntariness standard in *United States v. Coleman*, focusing specifically on Officer Kizer's statement: 'I'm sensing that we almost need to come inside.' We examine how the Seventh Circuit applied the *Bumper* and *Schneckloth* precedents to determine whether expressing an urgent 'need' constituted coercion or merely conveyed concern, and what this means for police training on requesting consent during high-stakes 911 calls.

blogs.title: The Matlock Dilemma: Third-Party Consent and the Dynamics of Domestic Violence Calls
blogs.description: While third-party consent under *United States v. Matlock* is settled law, its application in domestic violence scenarios presents unique tensions. This post explores the intersection of spousal consent and the defendant's privacy rights when the consenting party is the alleged victim. We discuss the significance of the wife's initial refusal ('I'd prefer you not') followed by her eventual consent, and how courts should weigh the power dynamics inherent in DV situations when assessing the validity of third-party permission.

blogs.title: From Welfare Check to Warrant: The Scope of Consent in *United States v. Coleman*
blogs.description: Once officers enter a home with consent, how far can they go before exceeding the scope of that permission? This post dissects the Seventh Circuit's application of the *Florida v. Jimeno* 'objective reasonableness' test. We analyze whether the officers' actions—locating the husband, speaking with the children about the gun, and scanning the home—remained within the bounds of a welfare check or if they effectively conducted a general search before securing a warrant.
